newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Britain outside the EU - survive, thrive, dive?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Britain outside the EU - survive, thrive, dive?.

text.p: Leaving the European Union will plunge Britain back into an economic dark age.
Leaving the European Union will have a marginally negative economic impact on Britain.
Leaving the European Union may have a positive economic impact on Britain.
These conflicting scenarios are all touted by academics and politicians as recent events raise the possibility that Britain may choose, or be forced to leave, the EU.
The arguments for and against have become part of a political game.
"You hear people starting from a position of prejudice, and finding figures to prove their point," said Professor Simon Coke from Edinburgh University's business school.
Some Britons worry about German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac's plan for an ever closer union of European states.
Remarks last month by Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda that countries not taking part in the EU's single currency might find it difficult attracting future foreign investment, added to the debate.
Toyota, and other Japanese car makers like Nissan and Honda have been huge investors in Britain.

On Tuesday, the chairman of the Anglo-Dutch consumer products giant Unilever was reported by the Guardian newspaper as saying the company might review its investments in Britain if it failed to sign up for monetary union.
"If Britain absented itself, that would certainly lead to reconsideration of certain investment decisions,..." Unilever chairman Niall FitzGerald was quoted as saying.

Some politicians argue that Okuda's remarks have demonstrated that Britain must join the single currency or its economic future would be blighted. Others say any further involvement with European Monetary Union risks further erosion of sovereignty.
It wouldn't only mean rule from Brussels, but apparently from Tokyo too.
DIVIDE OVER SINGLE CURRENCY

Britain's ruling Conservatives have been gingerly moving towards a more Eurosceptic position, but still won't say whether it would sign up for a single currency. The opposition Labour Party, well ahead in opinion polls and heavily favoured to win the election, says it would examine all the facts before deciding whether to sign up for the single currency.

If Britain decides not to join the single currency, many experts believe this means crisis for the EU. Britain could decide to pull out, or irate European leaders might force it to leave if they concluded this was the only way to achieve their dream of European unity.
Some experts say that Britain outside the EU would be enfeebled, forced out of European markets by a wall of tariffs.
COULD GATT AND THE WTO GUARANTEE FREE TRADE?

Others point to countries like the United States and Switzerland whose exports to the EU are booming. All they need is international trading agreements safeguarded by the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), and the World Trade Organisation (WTO). Britain could do just the same, they say.
Not so, says Paul Donovan, senior economist at Union Bank of Switzerland.

"If Britain were to be excluded from its trading bloc, and this is a very hypothetical scenario, it would have a severe impact on the U.K. economy. We would expect to see an immediate drying up of foreign direct investment there."
The average tariff on trade between industrialised countries dropped to just over six percent in 1995 from about 40 percent when GATT first started in 1948.

Under the terms of the Uruguay Round, average tariffs will fall to 3.8 percent in 1999. The proportion of industrial goods with a zero rating will rise to 44 percent in 1999 from 20 percent in 1995, according to the WTO.
But Donovan said GATT and WTO rules wouldn't be enough to guarantee free trade.
Martin Burridge, a lecturer in economics and international business at the Henley Management College, agrees.
"The WTO would not be able, in my view, to ensure a free trade flow between a Britain outside the EU," he said.

Foreign trade accounts for about 35 percent of Britain, France and Germany's economies, compared with about 14 percent for the U.S. and Japan, according to Burridge. This makes access to foreign markets more important for Britain than say, the U.S.
OTHER SIDE OF THE ARGUMENT
But life outside the EU is not seen as a problem by other economists such as Professor Anna Schwartz of New York's National Bureau of Economic Research.

"It's hard for me to understand why Britain's position would be any different from Switzerland or the U.S. I don't believe anything indicates that the single market will not be available if Britain doesn't accept a single currency," Schwartz said.

She is also unimpressed with the argument that companies would prefer to locate within the EU at the expense of Britain because European Monetary Union would produce a strong, stable currency, and low inflation.
"That is assuming a great deal. The single currency will have to prove itself," she said.
Professor Colin Robinson of Britain's right wing Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) agrees that the Euro might not be a successful currency.

"It is not a given. It could be the other way round. Britain could be the country with quite a strong currency with low interest rates compared with the rest of Europe if monetary union goes ahead and flounders," Robinson said.
And Robinson believes GATT and WTO rules would guarantee Britain's access to EU markets.

"These rules have been set after all to make sure there is free trade. If Britain wasn't in the EU the EU couldn't discriminate because of trade rules. They might find hidden ways to get around rules, but they do that anyway," Robinson said.
IEA SEES LITTLE ECONOMIC IMPACT IF BRITAIN LEAVES EU

The IEA sponsored a report published last year called "Better Off Out?" which concluded that the net effect of withdrawal on the British economy would be small -- probably less than one percent of Gross Domestic Product. "If a special relationship with the rest of the E.U. were arranged, there might be a small benefit", it concluded.
"We aren't arguing for withdrawal. We say if politicians decide (to leave) you don't have to worry about the economic costs because they would be quite small," Robinson said.

But Edinburgh University's Coke worries that European leaders, embittered by the failure of their vision of Europe, might be tempted to make life as difficult as possible for Britain. If comparative British economic success was said to be because of an unfair exchange rate, that might provide the catalyst for retaliation.
Gavin McCrone, visiting professor at Edinburgh University, sees disaster following withdrawal.

"These people (Toyota and other foreign investors) are only here because we are part of the European Union. They would quickly start switching investment to other countries. We would suffer quite badly if we tried to rupture ourselves out of Europe. And we couldn't rely on WTO and GATT to help us."
